front_blocks.md: Define **reversible reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants, meaning the reaction can proceed in both the **forward** and **reverse** directions.

cards.front_md: Define **reversible reaction**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The forward reaction in a reversible reaction forms the products.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The **forward reaction** converts reactants into products. In a reversible reaction, the **reverse reaction** converts those products back into reactants.

front_blocks.md: In a reversible reaction, the symbol **..........**  is used in the equation to show that the reaction can go in **..........**  directions.

back_blocks.md: In a reversible reaction, the symbol **⇌** is used in the equation to show that the reaction can go in **both** directions.

front_blocks.md: What happens when **ammonium chloride** is heated?

back_blocks.md: When **ammonium chloride** (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) is heated, it decomposes to form **ammonia** (NH<sub>3</sub>) and **hydrogen chloride** (HCl) gases. When the gases cool, they recombine to reform solid ammonium chloride.

front_blocks.md: What is **water of crystallisation**?

back_blocks.md: **Water of crystallisation** is water that is incorporated into the crystal structure of some salts, affecting their shape and colour.

front_blocks.md: What is the colour change when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated?

back_blocks.md: When hydrated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O) is heated, it loses its water of crystallisation and turns from **blue** to **white**, forming **anhydrous copper(II) sulfate**.

Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is blue.

Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is **white** (a white powder). It is the **hydrated** form, copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O), that appears blue.

front_blocks.md: Why do reversible reactions use the ⇌ symbol rather than a single arrow?

back_blocks.md: Reversible reactions use the ⇌ symbol to show that the reaction proceeds in **both directions** simultaneously. A single arrow would only indicate a one-way reaction going to **completion**.

front_blocks.md: Define **dynamic equilibrium**.

back_blocks.md: **Dynamic equilibrium** is the state reached in a **reversible reaction** when the rate of the **forward reaction** equals the rate of the **reverse reaction**, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

cards.front_md: Define **dynamic equilibrium**.
cards.back_md: **Dynamic equilibrium** is the state reached in a **reversible reaction** when the rate of the **forward reaction** equals the rate of the **reverse reaction**, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

front_blocks.md: What are the two key features of a system at **dynamic equilibrium**?

back_blocks.md: The two key features of a system at dynamic equilibrium are:

1. The rate of the **forward reaction** equals the rate of the **reverse reaction**
2. The **concentrations** of reactants and products remain constant

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Dynamic equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Dynamic equilibrium requires a **closed system** so that none of the reacting chemical species can escape and nothing else can enter the reaction vessel.

front_blocks.md: At the start of the Haber process, only nitrogen and hydrogen are present, so the rate of the **..........** reaction is at its highest. As ammonia builds up, the rate of the **..........** reaction increases.

back_blocks.md: At the start of the Haber process, only nitrogen and hydrogen are present, so the rate of the **forward** reaction is at its highest. As ammonia builds up, the rate of the **reverse** reaction increases.

front_blocks.md: Why does the rate of the forward reaction decrease as a reversible reaction proceeds?

back_blocks.md: As the reversible reaction proceeds, the concentrations of the **reactants** decrease. Since reaction rate depends on concentration, a lower concentration of reactants means the forward reaction slows down.

cards.front_md: Why does the rate of the forward reaction decrease as a reversible reaction proceeds?
cards.back_md: As the reversible reaction proceeds, the concentrations of the **reactants** decrease. Since reaction rate depends on concentration, a lower concentration of reactants means the forward reaction slows down.

front_blocks.md: What is a **closed system**?

back_blocks.md: A **closed system** is one in which no substances can enter or leave the reaction vessel, ensuring that all the reacting species remain present throughout the reaction.

cards.front_md: What is a **closed system**?
cards.back_md: A **closed system** is one in which no substances can enter or leave the reaction vessel, ensuring that all the reacting species remain present throughout the reaction.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
At dynamic equilibrium, reactants are completely used up.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
At dynamic equilibrium, the **concentrations** of both reactants and products remain constant — neither is fully used up. Both forward and **reverse reactions** continue at equal rates.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

At dynamic equilibrium, reactants are completely used up.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

At dynamic equilibrium, the **concentrations** of both reactants and products remain constant — neither is fully used up. Both forward and **reverse reactions** continue at equal rates.

front_blocks.md: Why is equilibrium described as **"dynamic"**?

back_blocks.md: Equilibrium is described as **dynamic** because the forward and reverse reactions are **still occurring** continuously, even though the overall concentrations of reactants and products appear unchanged.

cards.front_md: Why is equilibrium described as **"dynamic"**?
cards.back_md: Equilibrium is described as **dynamic** because the forward and reverse reactions are **still occurring** continuously, even though the overall concentrations of reactants and products appear unchanged.

front_blocks.md: How does a system at equilibrium respond to a change in conditions?

back_blocks.md: A system at **equilibrium** responds to **oppose** any change made to its conditions. The equilibrium shifts in the direction that counteracts the imposed change.

cards.front_md: How does a system at equilibrium respond to a change in conditions?

front_blocks.md: How does increasing the temperature affect an equilibrium reaction where the forward reaction is **exothermic**?

back_blocks.md: Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction of the **endothermic** reaction to oppose the change. If the forward reaction is exothermic, the equilibrium shifts to the **left**, favouring the reverse reaction and producing more reactants.

cards.front_md: How does increasing the temperature affect an equilibrium reaction where the forward reaction is **exothermic**?
cards.back_md: Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction of the **endothermic** reaction to oppose the change. If the forward reaction is exothermic, the equilibrium shifts to the **left**, favouring the reverse reaction and producing more reactants.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Increasing pressure always shifts the equilibrium to the right.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **fewer moles of gas**. If both sides have equal numbers of gas molecules, there is **no effect** on the position of equilibrium.

front_blocks.md: An increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with the **..........** number of gaseous molecules. A decrease in pressure shifts it towards the side with the **..........** number of gaseous molecules.

back_blocks.md: An increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with the **smallest** number of gaseous molecules. A decrease in pressure shifts it towards the side with the **greatest** number of gaseous molecules.

front_blocks.md: What does it mean when the position of equilibrium shifts to the right?

back_blocks.md: When the position of equilibrium shifts to the **right**, the **forward reaction** is favoured, meaning more **products** are formed and the concentration of reactants decreases.

cards.front_md: What does it mean when the position of equilibrium shifts to the right?

front_blocks.md: What is meant by the **position of equilibrium**?

back_blocks.md: The **position of equilibrium** describes the relative amounts of reactants and products present in a system at equilibrium. It indicates whether the equilibrium lies more to the **left** (more reactants) or to the **right** (more products).

cards.front_md: What is meant by the **position of equilibrium**?
cards.back_md: The **position of equilibrium** describes the relative amounts of reactants and products present in a system at equilibrium. It indicates whether the equilibrium lies more to the **left** (more reactants) or to the **right** (more products).

front_blocks.md: How does a **catalyst** affect the position of equilibrium?

back_blocks.md: A **catalyst** does not alter the **position of equilibrium**. It speeds up both the forward and **reverse reactions** by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached more quickly but the concentrations at equilibrium remain unchanged.

cards.front_md: How does a **catalyst** affect the position of equilibrium?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A catalyst shifts the position of equilibrium towards the products.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

A catalyst does not shift the position of equilibrium. It increases the rate of both the **forward** and **reverse reactions** equally, so the same equilibrium concentrations are reached, just more quickly.
